subject: Mechanisms
title: Surviving 100G Shock Loads in Cycloidal Drives

epitrochoid_curve.title: Epitrochoid Generation & Curvature Offset
epitrochoid_curve.body:
An epitrochoid is the mathematical path traced by a point at distance $R_{\text{cam}}$ from the center of a generating circle of radius $r$ rolling without slipping along the exterior of a stationary circle of radius $R$. Offsetting this curve by the roller pin radius $r_{\text{pin}}$ produces the cycloidal disc profile, ensuring continuous pure rolling contact without tooth undercut.

Epitrochoid Parametric Coordinate Equations:
$$x(\theta) = (R + r)\cos(\theta) - e \cdot \cos\left(\frac{R + r}{r}\theta\right)$$$$y(\theta) = (R + r)\sin(\theta) - e \cdot \sin\left(\frac{R + r}{r}\theta\right)$$
$e$: eccentric throw distance, $R$: base radius, $r$: rolling circle radius

hertzian_contact_stress.title: Hertzian Cylindrical Contact Stress
hertzian_contact_stress.body:
Because cycloidal pins and lobes maintain line contact, contact pressures are governed by Heinrich Hertz's elastic cylinder-on-cylinder equations. Peak compressive contact stress $\sigma_H$ is proportional to the square root of normal force divided by relative radius of curvature, whereas cantilever gear teeth experience shear and bending moment stresses that scale linearly with cantilever height.

Peak Hertzian Compressive Stress:
$$\sigma_H = \sqrt{\frac{F_n}{\pi \cdot L} \cdot \frac{\frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2}}{\frac{1 - \nu_1^2}{E_1} + \frac{1 - \nu_2^2}{E_2}}}$$
$F_n$: normal load per pin, $L$: pin contact length, $E_1, E_2$: Young's moduli (~210 GPa)

eccentric_offset.title: Eccentric Cam Throw & Centrifugal Imbalance
eccentric_offset.body: The eccentric cam offset $e$ dictates the cycloidal disc's epicyclic orbit radius. While small offsets ($e = 1.0\text{ to }2.5\text{ mm}$) generate high single-stage gear ratios, the orbiting mass creates rotating centrifugal unbalance force ($F_c = m \cdot e \cdot \omega_{\text{in}}^2$). Countering this requires dual discs phased 180° apart with matched balance counterweights.

strain_wave_gearing.title: Harmonic Strain Wave Drive Fragility
strain_wave_gearing.body: Harmonic drives utilize an elliptical wave generator inside a thin-walled flexible cup (flexspline). While delivering zero backlash and high ratios in compact envelopes, the flexspline wall is only 0.2 to 0.4 mm thick. Shock events exceeding 300% rated torque trigger catastrophic flexspline buckling or fatigue fracture.

needle_roller_bearing.title: Needle Roller Pin Bushings
needle_roller_bearing.body: To convert sliding friction to rolling friction, the stationary ring pins and output torque pins are sleeved with precision-ground needle roller bearings or rotating alloy steel sleeves (100Cr6 / 52100). This elevates mechanical efficiency above 92% and prevents micro-galling under 100G dynamic impulse spikes.

article_html:
ISSUE #000•MECHANISMS•14 MIN READ

Surviving 100G Shock Loads in Cycloidal Drives

How rolling pin contact and epitrochoidal tooth profiles distribute catastrophic shock loads across 30% of teeth simultaneously.

1. The Shock Load Paradox: Why Involute Gear Teeth Shear at 100G

In precision robotics, aerospace flight-surface actuators, and legged robotic quadruped limbs, actuation systems routinely encounter extreme kinetic shock loads. When a 45-kilogram humanoid or quadruped lands dynamically on concrete, or when an industrial articulated arm experiences an emergency stop collision at 2.5 m/s, ground reaction forces propagate backward into the joint gearbox at deceleration rates exceeding 50G to 100G.

In conventional high-precision gearing systems—such as multistage planetary gearheads or harmonic strain wave drives—these shock pulses are catastrophic:

  • Involute Cantilever Bending: In standard planetary gear sets, total contact ratio ($CR$) is typically between 1.2 and 1.6. At any discrete instant, all transmitted torque is carried by just one or two gear teeth acting as cantilevered trapezoidal beams. The root bending stress $\sigma_b$ scales according to the Lewis formula:
    $$\sigma_b = \frac{F_t}{b \cdot m \cdot Y}$$
    Under a 100G transient torque spike (often 500% to 1,000% of rated operating torque), the bending moment at the tooth root fillet exceeds the ultimate tensile yield strength of the carburized alloy steel, causing immediate plastic shear fracture and catastrophic stripping of the planet teeth.
  • Harmonic Flexspline Buckling: Harmonic drives achieve remarkable zero-backlash precision by elastically deforming a thin-walled alloy cup (flexspline) into an elliptical cam. However, because the flexspline wall thickness must remain razor-thin (typically 0.25 mm to 0.45 mm) to permit continuous elastic cyclic deflection, a 100G shock impulse causes instantaneous torsional buckling or brittle shear rupture across the cup diaphragm.

To achieve near-zero backlash, extreme torsional stiffness, and absolute survivability under 500% momentary shock overloads, kinematicians turned to a fundamentally different geometry: the cycloidal speed reducer.

2. Epitrochoidal Geometry: Rolling Pin Contact vs. Sliding Friction

The operating principle of a cycloidal drive eliminates conventional gear teeth entirely. In place of mating involute flanks that slide across one another, the mechanism pairs a cam disc contoured with an epitrochoid curve against an outer ring of cylindrical hardened steel roller pins.

Kinematic Generation: An epitrochoid is the geometric locus generated by a point attached to a rolling circle of radius $r$ as it rolls without slipping along the exterior circumference of a base circle of radius $R$. By offsetting the resulting mathematical path inward by the roller pin radius $r_{\text{pin}}$, we obtain the conjugate cycloidal tooth profile.

The fundamental reduction ratio $R_c$ of a single-stage cycloidal drive is governed by the difference between the number of stationary perimeter pins $N$ and the number of lobes $Z$ machined onto the cycloidal disc:

$$R_c = \frac{Z}{N - Z}$$

In standard industrial configurations, the cycloidal disc possesses exactly one fewer lobe than the stationary housing has pins ($Z = N - 1$). Substituting $N - Z = 1$ yields:

$$R_c = \frac{N - 1}{1} = N - 1$$

For example, a stationary ring housing containing $N = 30$ roller pins engaged with a cycloidal disc of $Z = 29$ lobes produces a single-stage speed reduction ratio of exactly 29:1 in an axial length of less than 35 mm. For every complete 360° rotation of the high-speed eccentric input shaft, the cycloidal disc advances by only one tooth pitch in the opposite direction.

3. Load Distribution Kinematics: The 30% Contact Engagement Rule

The defining engineering trait that endows cycloidal drives with extreme shock resistance is their multi-tooth load sharing behavior.

In an involute spur or planetary gear mesh, contact begins at the tip of the gear tooth and slides downward toward the pitch point, concentrating line load across a single tooth pair. If a sudden shock deceleration occurs, that lone tooth absorbs the entire impulse energy, frequently exceeding the material's yield point.

In stark contrast, because the cycloidal disc profile is conjugate to the entire perimeter array of pins, rotation of the eccentric shaft causes between 25% and 35% of all pins to engage simultaneously across the lower load-bearing half-arc.

Compressive vs. Bending Stress Distribution:

  • Elimination of Cantilever Bending: The cycloidal lobes do not project outward as unsupported cantilevers. Instead, the disc is a solid, monolithic wheel supported internally by heavy-duty cylindrical roller bearings. The force transmitted between each roller pin and the disc lobe acts purely as a normal compressive force perpendicular to the tangent of the epitrochoid curve.
  • Hertzian Contact Stress Mitigation: Under Hertzian contact theory, two convex cylinders pressed together distribute load across a rectangular contact patch of half-width $b_H$:
    $P_{\text{Hertz}} \approx \sqrt{\frac{F_n \cdot E^*}{\pi \cdot R_{\text{eff}} \cdot L}}$

    Physical Intuition: Peak contact stress scales with the square root of pin load ($F_n$). By concurrently sharing torque across 8 to 12 perimeter pins simultaneously, the cycloidal disc cuts contact stress below the carburized steel spalling limit without needing massive gear teeth.

    Because 8 to 12 pins share the total tangential load $F_t$ concurrently, the individual normal load $F_n$ per pin is reduced by nearly an order of magnitude:
    $$F_{n,\text{peak}} \approx \frac{2 \cdot T_{\text{output}}}{D_{\text{pitch}} \cdot (0.30 \cdot N)}$$
    Even during a violent 100G landing impact, the peak compressive stress $\sigma_H$ remains safely below the plastic yield limit of case-hardened alloy steels (typically $1{,}800\text{ to }2{,}200\text{ MPa}$).

4. Dynamic Balancing: Dual Counter-Phased Discs & Vibration Cancellation

While cycloidal reducers exhibit exceptional torque density and shock resistance, their eccentric orbit introduces a serious dynamic dilemma: centrifugal unbalance.

The input shaft is machined with an eccentric cam of throw $e$ (typically $1.0\text{ to }2.5\text{ mm}$). As the high-speed input motor spins at $3{,}000\text{ RPM}$ ($\omega_{\text{in}} \approx 314\text{ rad/s}$), the cycloidal disc orbits eccentrically around the gearbox center axis.

If only a single cycloidal disc were used, this orbiting mass $m_{\text{disc}}$ would generate an immense rotating centrifugal force vector:

$$F_c = m_{\text{disc}} \cdot e \cdot \omega_{\text{in}}^2$$

For a modest disc of mass $m = 0.65\text{ kg}$ with eccentric throw $e = 1.8\text{ mm}$ spinning at $3{,}000\text{ RPM}$:

$$F_c = 0.65 \cdot 0.0018 \cdot (314.16)^2 = 115.5\text{ Newtons}$$

This 115N rotating radial load would continuously hammer the input shaft bearings, generating unacceptable acoustic howling, severe vibration, and accelerated fatigue failure.

The 180° Dual-Disc Solution: Production cycloidal reducers solve this issue by stacking two identical cycloidal discs phased exactly 180° apart on a dual-lobe crankshaft. When Disc A translates upward and to the right, Disc B translates with identical momentum downward and to the left.

  • Dynamic Inertial Cancellation: Because the two equal masses move with identical velocity in opposite directions, the primary centrifugal forces sum precisely to zero:
    $$\sum \vec{F}_c = m \cdot \vec{a}_A + m \cdot \vec{a}_B = 0$$
  • Doubling Torque Capacity: Beyond dynamic balance, running dual discs doubles the total contact line length across the roller pins, reducing peak Hertzian contact stress by an additional 29% and doubling the ultimate fatigue life ($L_{10h}$).
  • Moment Couple Balancing: Because the two discs are separated by a small axial spacing $\Delta z$, they produce a secondary dynamic rocking moment ($M_{\text{couple}} = F_c \cdot \Delta z$). Precision reducers cancel this couple by integrating two counterweights on the high-speed input shaft positioned outside the disc pack.

5. Metallurgy & Surface Tribology: Case-Hardened 100Cr6 vs. AISI 8620

Because cycloidal reducers rely heavily on rolling line contact under extreme localized pressures, material selection, heat treatment, and surface tribology govern their operational longevity.

Material Pairings:

  • Roller Pins (AISI 52100 / 100Cr6 Bearing Steel): The perimeter ring pins and output torque rollers are manufactured from through-hardened 100Cr6 high-carbon chromium bearing alloy steel. Quenched and tempered to 60 to 64 HRC, 100Cr6 provides extreme yield strength ($R_{p0.2} > 1{,}700\text{ MPa}$) and high dimensional stability under cyclic contact stress. The pins are ground to a mirror surface finish of $Ra \le 0.10\;\mu\text{m}$ to minimize frictional torque.
  • Cycloidal Discs (AISI 8620 / 20NiCrMo2 Carburized Steel—a low-carbon nickel-chromium-molybdenum alloy steel engineered for extreme core toughness): The cycloidal discs undergo a deep vacuum carburizing process to create a hardened outer case (58 to 62 HRC, case depth $0.8\text{ to }1.2\text{ mm}$) overlying a ductile, impact-absorbing core (32 to 38 HRC, Charpy V-notch impact toughness $> 65\text{ J}$). This core ductility prevents catastrophic brittle fracture during violent 100G impact decelerations.

Elastohydrodynamic Lubrication (EHL): Under typical robotic duty cycles, the pitch-line rolling velocity creates a sub-micron hydrodynamic oil film (film thickness $h_c \approx 0.15\text{ to }0.45\;\mu\text{m}$) using fully synthetic Polyalphaolefin (PAO) grease thickened with lithium complex soap. Under 100G shock events, extreme pressure (EP) additives containing molybdenum disulfide ($\text{MoS}_2$) or sulfur-phosphorus compounds form sacrificial tribofilms, preventing metal-to-metal micro-welding and adhesion galling.

6. Spec Comparison Matrix: Cycloidal vs. Harmonic Strain Wave vs. Planetary

Selecting an actuator reducer requires balancing shock tolerance, zero-backlash precision, mass, and manufacturing cost:

7. First-Principles Summary: The Actuation Engineering Playbook

The physics of high-impact robotic actuation demonstrates that component geometry dictates survival. When shock forces surge into the hundred-G domain, relying on cantilever gear teeth invites mechanical disaster.

By replacing bending cantilevers with pure Hertzian compressive contact, and distributing impact energy across nearly a third of all contact points simultaneously, the cycloidal drive achieves what standard gearing cannot: near-zero backlash motion coupled with virtually indestructible overload survivability. For dynamic quadrupeds, robotic exoskeletons, and industrial automation where emergency impacts are inevitable, cycloidal architecture remains the premier mechanical standard.
